Feature 1: Forewing venation is trifid or quadrifid in many groups.
Feature 2: Tympanal hearing organs occur on the metathorax in many species.
Feature 3: Adults often have robust bodies and relatively narrow forewings.
Exceptions and caveats: Wing venation and tympanal anatomy require specialist examination; body shape overlaps other moth families.

Feature 1: Larvae typically have two pairs of abdominal prolegs and move by looping.
Feature 2: Adults often rest with wings spread flat.
Feature 3: Adults usually have relatively slender bodies and broad wings.
Exceptions and caveats: Some larvae have additional prolegs; resting posture and body shape are not exclusive.

Feature 1: Adults typically have robust streamlined bodies and long, narrow forewings.
Feature 2: Many species hover while feeding through a long proboscis.
Feature 3: Larvae frequently bear a horn near the posterior end.
Exceptions and caveats: Some adults have reduced mouthparts; larval horn may be absent or replaced by a button.

Feature 1: Antennae are usually long and filiform.
Feature 2: Hind trochanters are often conspicuously enlarged.
Feature 3: Adults often have prominent mandibles and striate elytra.
Exceptions and caveats: Many exceptions to general habitus; specialist structural characters are more reliable.

Feature 1: Adults are usually oval and convex dorsally.
Feature 2: Antennae are short, typically with a clubbed tip.
Exceptions and caveats: Some species are elongate or flattened; tarsal characters need magnification.

Feature 1: Antennae are often as long as or longer than the body.
Feature 2: Eyes are frequently notched around antennal insertions.
Feature 3: Tarsi are typically pseudotetramerous, with a reduced fourth segment.
Exceptions and caveats: Short-antenna species occur; characters are not exclusive to this family.

Feature 1: Floral reproductive structures are united into a column.
Feature 2: One petal is usually differentiated as a labellum.
Feature 3: Seeds are typically minute and dust-like.
Exceptions and caveats: Atypical floral morphologies occur; floral column is the strongest of these traits.

Feature 1: Small florets are grouped into a capitulum.
Feature 2: Anthers are usually united into a tube around the style.
Feature 3: The fruit is usually a cypsela, sometimes bearing a pappus.
Exceptions and caveats: Capitula vary greatly; pappus may be absent.

Feature 1: Leaves are often opposite and stems may be quadrangular.
Feature 2: Flowers are often tubular and bilabiate.
Feature 3: Fruits frequently form four nutlets, although drupaceous fruits also occur.
Exceptions and caveats: Square stems and two-lipped flowers are not universal; exceptions common.

Feature 1: Many species develop a universal veil that may leave a volva or cap remnants.
Feature 2: In typical Amanita species, gills are free from the stipe.
Feature 3: Gilled members generally have a white spore print.
Exceptions and caveats: These characters mainly describe Amanita, not necessarily all Amanitaceae.

Feature 1: Many species have tubes and pores beneath the cap rather than gills.
Feature 2: Fruiting bodies are often fleshy and stipitate.
Feature 3: Many members form ectomycorrhizal associations with plants.
Exceptions and caveats: Gilled and other atypical forms exist; ecological trait not diagnostic on its own.

Feature 1: Fruiting bodies may be bracket-like, crust-like or stalked.
Feature 2: The hymenophore is often poroid, sometimes maze-like or lamellate.
Feature 3: Many species decompose wood, commonly causing white rot.
Exceptions and caveats: Strong convergence with other polypore families; family boundaries depend on phylogeny.
